summary: This document defines Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) labels for STUN usages, such as TURN and NAT discovery. These labels let an application negotiate which STUN usage will run over a TLS connection.

plainLanguage.summary: Before two computers talk, they must agree what language to use. This document makes name tags for the languages used to get around home routers.

subtitle: Defines labels for STUN protocols during TLS negotiation.

tldr.problem: STUN over TLS must identify which STUN usage (TURN, NAT discovery, etc.) will run on the connection, but no standard labels exist.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7443 registers two ALPN labels with IANA: 'stun.turn' for Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) and 'stun.nat-discovery' for NAT detection.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now negotiate STUN usages during TLS handshake without adding extra round trips, simplifying protocol implementation.

today: RFC 7443 is an Internet Standard. ALPN labels for STUN are now registered with IANA and used by applications implementing TURN and NAT discovery over TLS/DTLS.

sections.title: ALPN for STUN Protocols
sections.content: STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) is a protocol that helps applications discover whether they are behind a firewall and how to reach other hosts. STUN is now commonly run over TLS (for confidentiality) or DTLS (for datagrams). Applications using STUN have different purposes: TURN relays traffic, while other usages discover the local address. ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) is an extension to TLS that lets endpoints agree on which application protocol will run over a connection. The client sends a list of supported protocols, and the server chooses one. RFC 7443 registers ALPN labels for STUN usages so the negotiation can happen during the TLS handshake without extra messages.
sections.plainLanguage: When computers make a secure connection, they can tell each other what kind of traffic will flow through it. This document names the NAT-discovery services that use TLS.

sections.title: The ALPN Labels
sections.content: Two ALPN labels are registered. The label 'stun.turn' identifies STUN used for TURN: a relay service that forwards traffic when direct connections fail. The label 'stun.nat-discovery' identifies STUN used for discovering the address and port seen from outside a NAT box. Both labels work with TLS and DTLS. Endpoints include these labels in the ClientHello during the TLS handshake, and the server selects the one it supports.
sections.plainLanguage: 'stun.turn' means the connection will relay traffic. 'stun.nat-discovery' means it will check what your address looks like from outside.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: The ALPN extension for STUN introduces no new security considerations beyond what RFC 7301 (the ALPN specification) already defines. The labels themselves do not affect TLS/DTLS security, and they do not impact session establishment or application data exchange. Applications should follow the security guidance in the underlying STUN, TURN, and TLS/DTLS specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: These labels are just names and do not change how secure the connection is.
